questions.stem: The goal of full employment is generally taken to mean:
options: every person aged 15 and over working full-time hours
a participation rate of 100 per cent of the civilian population aged 15 and over
the lowest unemployment rate that can be sustained without inflation accelerating
an unemployment rate of zero, with every job seeker in work
questions.explanation: Full employment does not mean zero unemployment, because some frictional and structural unemployment always exists. It is the lowest rate the economy can sustain without wage and price pressures building.

questions.stem: The NAIRU is best described as the unemployment rate:
options: consistent with a stable rate of inflation
at which the federal budget is exactly balanced
that exists at the trough of the business cycle
reached once all frictional unemployment has been removed from the labour market
questions.explanation: NAIRU stands for the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment. Below it, labour shortages push wages and inflation up; at it, inflation is stable. It includes frictional unemployment rather than requiring its removal.

questions.stem: When the economy is at the NAIRU, the unemployment that remains is mainly:
options: cyclical and frictional unemployment
cyclical and structural unemployment
frictional and structural unemployment
cyclical unemployment
questions.explanation: At the NAIRU there is no cyclical unemployment, because demand is strong enough to employ everyone whose skills and location match available jobs. Frictional and structural unemployment remain.

questions.stem: If the unemployment rate falls well below the NAIRU, the most likely consequence is:
options: falling inflation as firms gain productivity from new workers
an increase in cyclical unemployment in the following year
a fall in the participation rate as workers leave the labour force
rising wage pressure that pushes the inflation rate higher
questions.explanation: Below the NAIRU, firms compete for scarce workers by offering higher wages, and those costs are passed on as higher prices. That is why unemployment that is too low is a risk to the inflation goal.

questions.stem: Under ABS definitions, a person is counted as employed if, in the reference week, they:
options: worked at least 35 hours in a full-time job
were registered with a government employment service
were actively looking for work and available to start
worked for one hour or more for pay, profit or payment in kind
questions.explanation: The ABS counts anyone who worked at least one hour for pay in the reference week as employed. Working 35 hours or more is the threshold for full-time work, not for being employed.

questions.stem: To be classed as unemployed, a person must be without work and have:
options: been out of work for at least 12 months and be receiving a government income support payment
received an unemployment benefit from the government at some time in the past four weeks
worked fewer than 15 hours in the reference week and want to work more hours
actively looked for work in the past four weeks and be available to start in the reference week
questions.explanation: The ABS measure requires a person to be without work, actively seeking work and available to start. Receiving a benefit is not part of the definition, and someone who worked some hours but wants more is underemployed.

questions.stem: Ruth wants a job but has stopped looking, because she believes none is available. Under ABS definitions she is:
options: long-term unemployed, because she has given up looking
hidden unemployed and not counted in the labour force
unemployed, because she would like to have a job
underemployed, because she is not working full-time
questions.explanation: Because Ruth is not actively looking for work, she is outside the labour force and not counted as unemployed. Discouraged job seekers like her are part of hidden unemployment.

questions.stem: Kai works 12 hours a week in retail and would like, and is available, to work more hours. He is classed as:
options: not in the labour force
employed and underemployed
unemployed
hidden unemployed
questions.explanation: Kai worked at least one hour, so he is employed, but he wants and is available for more hours, so he is also underemployed. Underemployed workers are part of the labour force under-utilisation rate.

questions.stem: Long-term unemployment refers to people who have been unemployed for:
options: four weeks or more
two years or more
12 months or more
6 months or more
questions.explanation: People unemployed for a year or more are classed as long-term unemployed. Long spells out of work erode skills and confidence, making it harder to find work again.

questions.stem: A software engineer leaves one job and spends three weeks searching before starting a better-matched job. During those three weeks she is:
options: structurally unemployed
cyclically unemployed
hidden unemployed
frictionally unemployed
questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is the short period people spend between jobs while searching and matching. It is not caused by a fall in demand or a mismatch of skills.

questions.stem: An automotive plant closes because of changes in technology and global competition, and its workers' skills do not match the jobs now available. The resulting unemployment is:
options: hidden unemployment
structural unemployment
cyclical unemployment
frictional unemployment
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment comes from long-term changes in the structure of the economy that leave workers' skills or locations mismatched with available jobs. It does not end when demand recovers, so retraining is often needed.

questions.stem: Unemployment that rises because aggregate demand falls during a downturn in the business cycle is called:
options: long-term unemployment
cyclical unemployment
structural unemployment
frictional unemployment
questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment is caused by insufficient spending in the economy, so firms need fewer workers. It falls again as aggregate demand recovers.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes cyclical from structural unemployment?
options: Both types are counted within the NAIRU, so neither can be reduced by any government policy
Cyclical unemployment stems from weak aggregate demand; structural from a mismatch of skills or location
Cyclical unemployment usually needs retraining to fix, while structural ends when demand recovers
Cyclical unemployment arises from technological change, while structural follows the business cycle
questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment rises and falls with spending, so aggregate demand policies can reduce it. Structural unemployment comes from changes in the economy's structure and is part of the NAIRU, so it needs supply-side measures such as training.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical economy, the civilian population aged 15 and over is 20 million, 13 million people are employed and 0.6 million are unemployed. The participation rate is:
options: 4.4 per cent
3 per cent
68 per cent
65 per cent
questions.explanation: The labour force is 13 + 0.6 = 13.6 million, and 13.6 ÷ 20 × 100 = 68 per cent. Using only the employed gives 65 per cent, which leaves out the unemployed, who are part of the labour force.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical economy, 13.44 million people are employed and 0.56 million are unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
options: 0.4 per cent
4.0 per cent
4.2 per cent
5.6 per cent
questions.explanation: The labour force is 13.44 + 0.56 = 14 million, and 0.56 ÷ 14 × 100 = 4.0 per cent. Dividing by the number employed instead of the labour force gives about 4.2 per cent.

questions.stem: The unemployment rate is 4 per cent and the underemployment rate is 6 per cent. The labour force under-utilisation rate is:
options: 6 per cent
2 per cent
24 per cent
10 per cent
questions.explanation: The under-utilisation rate adds the unemployed and the underemployed as a share of the labour force: 4 + 6 = 10 per cent. It shows spare labour that the unemployment rate alone misses.

questions.stem: The unemployment rate falls from 5.0 per cent to 4.8 per cent, but the number of people employed is unchanged. The most likely explanation is that:
options: underemployed workers were given more hours by their employers
some unemployed people stopped looking for work and left the labour force
more people found jobs during the period and moved from unemployment into work
the participation rate rose as more people joined the labour force
questions.explanation: If employment is unchanged, the rate can only fall because fewer people are counted as unemployed, which here means some left the labour force. That is a rise in hidden unemployment rather than an improvement in the labour market.

questions.stem: As the population ages, a growing number of people retire. Other things being equal, this tends to:
options: lower the participation rate
raise the unemployment rate
raise the participation rate
raise hidden unemployment
questions.explanation: Retirees remain in the civilian population aged 15 and over but leave the labour force, so the labour force shrinks relative to the population. They are not looking for work, so they are neither unemployed nor hidden unemployed.

questions.stem: Unemployment well above the NAIRU harms the economy because it:
options: raises the participation rate as discouraged workers return to job search
improves the budget balance as the government collects more income tax
means lost output, lower tax revenue and higher spending on income support
pushes up wages and the inflation rate as firms compete hard for the workers available
questions.explanation: Idle workers produce nothing, so real GDP is lower than it could be, and the government collects less tax while paying more in benefits. Rising wage pressure is the risk when unemployment is too low.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-material cost of long-term unemployment for the individual?
options: Lower income tax payments to the government
Loss of self-esteem and a higher risk of mental illness
Lower disposable income for the household
Reduced ability to buy goods and services
questions.explanation: Long spells of unemployment can damage confidence, relationships and mental health, which are non-material living standards. Lower income and reduced spending are material costs.

questions.stem: Inflation is best defined as:
options: a rise in the prices of imported goods only
a sustained increase in the general level of prices
a once-off rise in the price of a single good
a sustained fall in the general level of prices
questions.explanation: Inflation is an ongoing rise in the average level of prices across the economy, which reduces the purchasing power of money. A price rise in one good is a change in relative prices, not inflation.

questions.stem: If the inflation rate falls from 5 per cent to 3 per cent, the economy is experiencing:
options: price stability, with the price level unchanged
disinflation, with prices rising more slowly
deflation, with the price level falling
rising inflation, with prices rising faster
questions.explanation: Disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation while prices are still rising. Deflation would require the price level itself to fall, which means a negative inflation rate.

questions.stem: Over a year, the CPI falls from 120.0 to 118.8. The economy has experienced:
options: deflation of 1.2 per cent
inflation of 1.0 per cent
deflation of 1.0 per cent
disinflation of 1.0 per cent
questions.explanation: The change is (118.8 − 120.0) ÷ 120.0 × 100 = −1.0 per cent, so the price level fell, which is deflation. The 1.2 is the change in index points, not the percentage change.

questions.stem: The goal of low and stable inflation is valued mainly because it:
options: prevents the exchange rate from changing in value
lets households and firms plan spending and investment without prices distorting their decisions
keeps the price of every good and service in the economy unchanged from one year to the next
guarantees that wages always rise faster than prices
questions.explanation: Low and stable inflation preserves purchasing power and makes future prices predictable, so decisions are based on real costs and returns. It allows relative prices to change, so it does not mean every price stays fixed.

questions.stem: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures changes in:
options: the prices that overseas buyers pay for Australia's exports
the prices of a basket of goods and services bought by households
the prices that Australian producers pay for raw materials and other inputs
the total value of all goods and services produced in Australia
questions.explanation: The ABS tracks the prices of a weighted basket of goods and services that households typically buy, and the CPI shows how the cost of that basket changes. Producer input prices and export prices are measured by other indexes.

questions.stem: The CPI rises from 140.0 to 144.2 over a year. The rate of inflation is:
options: 44.2 per cent
3.0 per cent
4.2 per cent
2.9 per cent
questions.explanation: Inflation is (144.2 − 140.0) ÷ 140.0 × 100 = 3.0 per cent. The 4.2 is the change in index points, and dividing by the later figure of 144.2 gives about 2.9 per cent, the wrong base.

questions.stem: Headline inflation differs from underlying (core) inflation in that headline inflation:
options: is adjusted to remove the effects of changes in the exchange rate
includes every item in the CPI basket, including those with volatile prices
excludes volatile items, such as fuel and fruit, to show the persistent trend
measures only the prices of services bought by households, not goods
questions.explanation: Headline inflation is the change in the full CPI. Underlying measures strip out or down-weight the most volatile price changes to show the persistent trend in inflation.

questions.stem: A cyclone destroys banana crops and fuel prices spike briefly, while most other prices rise steadily. Compared with underlying inflation, headline inflation is most likely to be:
options: lower, as temporary price shocks are given smaller weights in the headline measure
higher, as it includes the volatile price rises that underlying measures remove
lower, as volatile items such as bananas and fuel are excluded from the headline rate
the same, as both measures are calculated from the full CPI basket without adjustment
questions.explanation: Headline inflation includes the large, temporary rises in bananas and fuel. Underlying measures remove such extreme movements, so they show a lower, steadier rate in this case.

questions.stem: Policymakers watch underlying inflation closely because it:
options: measures inflation in the prices of imported goods and services only
is the only measure of inflation that the ABS publishes
gives a better guide to persistent inflation by removing temporary price movements
is always higher than headline inflation, so it gives an early warning
questions.explanation: Policy responds to lasting price pressures rather than one-off shocks, and underlying measures filter out much of the short-term volatility. Underlying inflation can be above or below the headline rate.

questions.stem: Demand inflation occurs when:
options: the Australian dollar appreciates against other major currencies
productivity grows faster than wages across most industries
aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's capacity to supply
costs of production rise and firms pass them on to consumers in higher prices
questions.explanation: Demand inflation, also called demand-pull inflation, occurs when spending outstrips the economy's ability to produce, so firms raise prices. Rising costs passed on to consumers describe cost inflation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause cost inflation?
options: A sharp rise in the world price of oil
Strong growth in household spending
A fall in average wages across industries
Faster growth in labour productivity
questions.explanation: Oil is a key input for transport and production, so a rise in its price lifts costs throughout the economy, and firms pass these on. Strong household spending causes demand inflation instead.

questions.stem: Average wages rise by 5 per cent in a year while labour productivity rises by 1 per cent. This is most likely to:
options: lower unit labour costs, easing pressure on prices
cause deflation, as firms cut prices to sell more
reduce inflation, as productivity growth offsets the wage rise
raise unit labour costs, adding to cost inflation
questions.explanation: When wages grow faster than output per worker, the labour cost of each unit of output rises by roughly 4 per cent. Firms tend to pass this on in higher prices, which is cost inflation.

questions.stem: Workers expect inflation to rise, so they bargain for higher wages, which firms then pass on in higher prices. This process is known as:
options: the substitution effect
structural unemployment
a wage-price spiral
disinflation
questions.explanation: In a wage-price spiral, higher expected inflation leads to higher wage claims, which raise costs and prices, which in turn raise expectations again. It can make inflation self-sustaining.

questions.stem: A large depreciation of the Australian dollar adds to inflation mainly because:
options: Australian exports become dearer for foreign buyers to purchase
interest rates on Australia's foreign debt fall as the dollar weakens
Australians buy more imports, lowering spending on local goods
imported goods and inputs become dearer in Australian dollars
questions.explanation: A lower dollar means each unit of foreign currency costs more Australian dollars, so imported goods and inputs rise in price. That feeds directly into the CPI and into firms' costs.

questions.stem: A worker's nominal wage rises by 2 per cent while inflation is 4 per cent. Her real wage:
options: is unchanged in real terms
falls by about 2 per cent
rises by about 2 per cent
rises by about 6 per cent
questions.explanation: The real wage changes by roughly the nominal wage rise minus inflation: 2 − 4 = −2 per cent. Prices are rising faster than her pay, so her purchasing power falls.

questions.stem: Unexpectedly high inflation tends to benefit:
options: borrowers with fixed-rate loans, as the real value of their debt falls
lenders who have lent money at a fixed rate of interest for many years
pensioners whose payments are fixed in dollar terms
savers who hold their wealth in cash
questions.explanation: Inflation erodes the real value of money, so a fixed debt becomes easier to repay in real terms. Lenders, people on fixed incomes and holders of cash lose purchasing power.

questions.stem: High and unpredictable inflation can lower the quality of investment in an economy because:
options: it guarantees higher real returns on productive capital such as factories
it encourages savers to hold more of their wealth as cash
uncertainty makes planning harder and diverts funds into speculative assets
it lowers the nominal cost of borrowing for every firm in the economy
questions.explanation: When future prices are hard to predict, firms delay long-term projects and investors favour assets such as property that may hold their value, rather than productive investment. That distortion of spending and investment decisions is a cost of high inflation.

questions.stem: If Australia's inflation rate is persistently higher than its trading partners', Australian exporters are likely to:
options: gain market share overseas, because higher prices signal higher quality
be unaffected, because inflation influences only domestic prices
lose international competitiveness, as their prices rise faster than rivals'
gain international competitiveness, as their revenue rises faster than rivals'
questions.explanation: If Australian prices rise faster than competitors' prices, Australian goods become relatively dearer in world markets. Other things being equal, exporters lose sales to foreign rivals.

questions.stem: A term deposit pays 4 per cent interest a year while inflation is 5 per cent. The saver's real return is about:
options: 1 per cent, so the deposit gains purchasing power
9 per cent, as the interest and inflation combine
4 per cent, as the nominal interest rate is fixed
−1 per cent, so the deposit loses purchasing power
questions.explanation: The real return is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation: 4 − 5 = −1 per cent. The saver ends the year with more dollars that buy less, which is the lower return on investment that high inflation causes.

questions.stem: Persistent deflation can harm the economy mainly because:
options: firms raise their output to take advantage of steadily falling costs of production
consumers delay spending while they wait for lower prices, so demand and jobs weaken
the real burden of existing debt falls, which encourages households to borrow excessively
Australian exports become uncompetitive as Australian prices fall relative to others
questions.explanation: If people expect prices to keep falling, they postpone purchases, so spending, output and employment fall. Deflation actually raises the real burden of debt and would make exports cheaper, not less competitive.
